title: Represent and operate on complex numbers in non-trivial situations

lessons.title: What complex numbers are and how to represent them
lessons.html:
Beyond real numbers

Some equations have no real-number solution. For example, x² + 1 = 0 would need a number whose square is −1. Mathematicians defined the imaginary unit i with the property i² = −1. A complex number is any number of the form z = a + bi, where a and b are real numbers.

  • a is the real part, written Re(z).
  • b is the imaginary part, written Im(z).
  • If b = 0, the number is real. If a = 0 and b ≠ 0, it is purely imaginary.

Where they are used

Complex numbers are used in electrical engineering for alternating current (AC) circuits, for example the electricity supply to farm pumps, motors and irrigation controllers, where voltage and current change direction many times a second. Engineers combine resistance and reactance into a complex impedance. They are also used in signal processing, control systems and physics.

The Argand diagram

A complex number can be drawn as a point on a plane: the horizontal axis is the real axis and the vertical axis is the imaginary axis. The number 3 + 4i is the point (3; 4).

Modulus and argument

The modulus |z| is the distance from the origin: |z| = √(a² + b²). For 3 + 4i, |z| = √(9 + 16) = 5.

The argument θ is the angle the line from the origin makes with the positive real axis: tan θ = b/a, taking care to choose the correct quadrant. For 3 + 4i, θ ≈ 53,1°.

Polar form

Using the modulus r and argument θ, z = r(cos θ + i sin θ). So 3 + 4i ≈ 5(cos 53,1° + i sin 53,1°). Polar form is especially useful for multiplying and dividing.

The conjugate

The conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi. On the Argand diagram it is the reflection in the real axis. Note that z × z̄ = a² + b², a real number.

lessons.title: Operations with complex numbers
lessons.html:
Calculating with complex numbers

Addition and subtraction

Add or subtract real parts and imaginary parts separately.

(3 + 4i) + (1 − 2i) = 4 + 2i

(3 + 4i) − (1 − 2i) = 2 + 6i

Multiplication

Multiply out the brackets and replace i² with −1.

(3 + 4i)(1 − 2i) = 3 − 6i + 4i − 8i² = 3 − 2i + 8 = 11 − 2i

In polar form, multiply the moduli and add the arguments: r₁r₂[cos(θ₁ + θ₂) + i sin(θ₁ + θ₂)].

Division

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.

(3 + 4i) ÷ (1 − 2i) = (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) ÷ [(1 − 2i)(1 + 2i)] = (3 + 6i + 4i + 8i²) ÷ (1 + 4) = (−5 + 10i) ÷ 5 = −1 + 2i

In polar form, divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

Powers of i

PowerValue
i¹i
i²−1
i³−i
i⁴1

The pattern repeats every four powers.

Solving quadratic equations

For ax² + bx + c = 0, if the discriminant b² − 4ac is negative, the roots are complex conjugates. Example: x² − 4x + 13 = 0. The discriminant is 16 − 52 = −36, so x = (4 ± √−36) ÷ 2 = (4 ± 6i) ÷ 2 = 2 ± 3i.

Applied example: AC impedance

An irrigation pump motor circuit has resistance 6 Ω and inductive reactance 8 Ω. Its impedance is Z = 6 + 8i Ω (engineers often write j instead of i). The magnitude |Z| = √(36 + 64) = 10 Ω. With a 230 V supply, the current magnitude is 230 ÷ 10 = 23 A.

Key points

  • i² = −1 and a complex number is a + bi.
  • The modulus is √(a² + b²); the argument is the angle from the positive real axis.
  • Add and subtract parts separately; multiply by expanding and using i² = −1.
  • Divide by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator.
  • Quadratics with negative discriminants have complex conjugate roots.
